records.text: A chapter of the Move Weight Foundation Welcome to ExposeMiamiOK! 🎉 Your voice matters in our community Thank You for Joining Us, {{EMAIL}}! You've just taken an important step toward building a stronger, more transparent Miami, Oklahoma. We're thrilled to have you as part of our growing community of engaged citizens. Subscribed on: {{DATE}} 🤝 We Need Your Help! Miami is at a crossroads. We're organizing volunteers to attend city council meetings, collect signatures for a mayoral recall, and fight against the proposed tax increases that could bankrupt Ottawa County. Every voice counts. Every signature matters. Every meeting attended makes a difference. Ready to Get Involved? Here's how you can help right now: Join Volunteer Team View County Resources 📚 What You Can Do: Attend City Council Meetings — Your presence shows elected officials that we're watching and we care Collect Signatures — Help us reach our goal for the mayoral recall petition Spread the Word — Share ExposeMiamiOK.com with friends, family, and neighbors Stay Informed — Read our blog posts about local government transparency and accountability Ask Questions — Use our open records request tools to demand transparency This isn't just a website — it's a movement. A community of neighbors who believe that Miami deserves better. Better transparency, better accountability, and better leadership. Whether you've lived here your whole life or just moved to town, whether you're young or old, whether you've been involved in local politics before or this is your first time — you belong here . This is a true melting pot where everyone's voice matters. Together, we're building something special. With gratitude, The ExposeMiamiOK Team A project of the MoveWeight Foundation, a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization dedicated to civic engagement and government transparency. records.summary: Moderated status page for Facebook-connected public-source captures.
records.text: Facebook Archive Review - ExposeMiamiOK Moderated archive Facebook Archive Review This page replaces the dead archive link. Legacy Facebook captures and current Promote4.me/Facebook leads are retained for staff review, but raw names, screenshots, and personal claims are no longer indexed publicly without moderation. Open public monitor Staff dashboard -- Monitored posts -- Pending review 0 Published allegations What Happened To The Old Posts? Older Facebook post pages may still exist as internal capture records, but the public archive now points here so visitors see the moderation policy first. For public use, ExposeMiamiOK should publish records, official links, meeting clips, and reviewed summaries. For staff use, the admin dashboard can still review the raw queue and decide whether a lead deserves a FOIA request or public record note. Raw social-media captures are not public evidence until reviewed. Use FOIA and official-source links for claims that need proof.

Law can prohibit a transaction, punish participants, seize proceeds, and establish investigative authority. It cannot, by declaration alone, eliminate demand, scarcity, desperation, profit, or corruption. The continued existence of illicit controlled-substance markets, human trafficking, illegal gambling, commercial sexual exploitation, weapons trafficking, and money laundering demonstrates that prohibition often changes the organization of a market rather than abolishing it. The canonical Gospels never describe Jesus as marrying, courting, or entering a romantic relationship. Christian tradition has therefore understood his earthly life as celibate. Yet celibacy does not necessarily imply emotional incapacity, freedom from attraction, or ignorance of the longing that accompanies human love. The deeper theological question is not whether Jesus secretly maintained a romance, for the evidence does not support such a claim, but whether the incarnate Son could have experienced romantic desire, unfulfilled affection, or love that could not be consummated. Any serious answer must begin with the Christian doctrine of the Incarnation. Jesus was not merely God appearing in human form. He was, according to orthodox Christian teaching, truly God and truly man. The Gospel of John declares that “the Word became flesh,” while the Epistle to the Hebrews describes him as one who shared fully in human weakness and was “tempted in all points” as humanity is, yet remained without sin. His humanity was not theatrical, partial, or insulated from ordinary emotion. He hungered, thirsted, tired, rejoiced, grieved, wept, suffered abandonment, and desired companionship. Key review points include the $97,879,083 budget resolution total, $82,728,742.05 in stated expenditures, the $689,440.01 June 2 claims list, MSUA transfers/carryover, and broad City Manager budget-transfer authority. Open packet audit PDF copy Text transcript Official source ⚠️ Read This First ExposeMiamiOK.com is independent. We are not affiliated with Ron Durbin, Guerrilla News, the City of Miami, Ottawa County, or any political candidate. Period. Everything on this site is organized from public records, court filings, news reports, meeting video, and government websites. We collect it in one place so residents can review the source material without hunting across a dozen systems. Views expressed in linked content belong to their creators. We do not endorse third-party claims; we preserve links and context so readers can check the record themselves. 🏛️ Miami, Oklahoma - records, services, and useful links A practical directory for city services, public records, meetings, court search, local news, and resident tools. 🗳️ Voter Registration & Elections Check registration, confirm your polling place, and keep local elections on your calendar. Register to Vote → Check Status → 📋 City Government Find city departments, staff contacts, official notices, and the public offices responsible for local services. Staff Directory → 📅 Meetings & Agendas 508 meetings. 107+ transcripts. Every council session from 2016 to now — searchable, watchable, and ready for a close read. Browse All Meetings → Calendar → Alerts → Web TV → 💼 Employment & Bids Track hiring, bids, purchasing, and contract opportunities from official city sources. City Jobs → Bids & RFPs → 🔧 Service Requests Potholes, code violations, streetlights out — report it. Whether they fix it is another story. Submit Request → Ask the City → 💰 Budget & Finance $97 million budget adopted June 2026. See where your tax dollars actually go. FY2026-27 Budget → Financial Docs → 📄 Documents & Forms Ordinances, permits, public records. The paper trail matters. Document Center → Forms → 🏫 Miami Public Schools K-12 public schools. Because an educated citizenry is harder to fool. District Website → 📚 Miami Public Library Books, internet, programs — free. One of the few things this town gets right. Library Website → 🎓 NEO A&M College Community college right here in town. Affordable degree path, no commute. NEO Website → Admissions → 🚨 Emergency: 911 For actual emergencies — police, fire, medical — dial 911 . Mental Health Crisis: 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) 🏥 Integris Miami Hospital Hospital, ER, medical services. You hope you never need it, but it's there. Integris Miami → 👮 Miami Police Department Non-emergency: (918) 542-2411 . For animal-control issues, confirm current after-hours response steps with dispatch or the city. Staff Directory → 🚒 Miami Fire Department Fire, EMS, prevention. These folks actually show up when you call. Contact Info → ⚖️ Ottawa County Court Clerk Court filings, records, licenses. OSCN has the dockets — search everything. Ottawa County Courts → 🌳 Parks & Recreation Parks, rec centers, events. The one city department nobody complains about. Parks Info → 🎣 Visit Miami OK Tourism, Route 66 history, attractions, and local places worth knowing beyond the headlines. Visit Miami → 📝 Open Records Requests Oklahoma Open Records Act means you can see what they're doing. Use it. They hate that. How to Request → 🏗️ Building Permits Permits, inspections, requirements. Build by the book or pay for it later. Permits → Inspections → 💵 Fee Schedule What everything costs. Water, sewer, permits, fines — all of it. Fee Schedule → 👥 Boards & Commissions Boards, committees, citizen seats. If you want change, get on one. Boards → Apply → 🔍 Transparency The city's own transparency portal. Compare what they say to what we've found. Transparent Miami → 🌾 OSU Extension Ag education, 4-H, family programs. OSU's local presence — solid resource. OSU Extension → 🐾 Animal Services Adoptions, lost pets, rescues. Also: the same department whose director threatened a citizen with prosecution for complaining about dog attacks. Animal Services → 📜 History of Miami British Flyers, Spartan School, Route 66. Miami has real history worth knowing. History → 🪦 Cemetery Cemetery records and info. Cemetery → 🎖️ Fallen Heroes Fallen first responders and military — honored here. Fallen Heroes → 🗺️ Maps Maps, zoning, floodplains. Know your property before the city tells you about it. If you have source material about fraud, waste, abuse, or public-records issues in Miami or Ottawa County, preserve it and send it through a channel you trust. FBI Oklahoma City: (405) 290-7770 🗺️ Miami, Oklahoma & Surrounding Area Surrounding Communities 📍 Miami County seat, pop. ~13,000 📍 Commerce Pop. ~2,500 📍 Afton Pop. ~1,000 📍 Fairland Pop. ~1,200 📍 Quapaw Pop. ~900 📍 North Miami Pop. ~400 🤝 Sick of This? Do Something About It. You can help by reading source documents, attending public meetings, saving records, and sharing corrections when something needs more context. 🎯 Here's What Actually Moves the Needle: ✓ Show up to council meetings — an empty room is a room they control ✓ File FOIA requests — it's your right and they hate it ✓ Send us tips, documents, recordings — anything you've got ✓ Share this site with neighbors who want source-linked local information ✓ Vote like this town depends on it, because it does Get Involved See What We've Found → 🏛️ Ottawa County: The Full Picture Every county office, every form, every public record — and the $40 million wrongful death judgment they're still figuring out how to pay. Dig Into Ottawa County → ℹ️ About This Project Why does this site exist? Because the city of Miami, Oklahoma has a transparency problem, and nobody else was documenting it. This site is run by the MoveWeight Foundation, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. We aggregate public records, meeting transcripts, court filings, news coverage, and watchdog reporting — all in one place. No login. No paywall. No ads. This started with one question: why is it so hard to know what your own city government is doing? We are building practical tools to answer that question: FOIA submission, public-source monitoring, crime feed, meeting transcripts, evidence archives, and plain-language links back to original records. How It Works 🔍 Data Collection We scrape, download, and archive public information from government sites, YouTube feeds, court databases, and news outlets. If it's public, we collect it before it disappears. 🎯 Smart Filtering We filter for Miami and Ottawa County relevance. No clickbait, no out-of-state noise — just what matters here. 🌐 Open Access Everything we publish is already public record. We just organize it so you can actually find it and use it. 🔍 Transparency & Data Sources ✅ Where This Comes From Every claim on this site is sourced from: • City of Miami official website (miamiok.gov) • YouTube RSS feeds (public data) • Ottawa County court records (OSCN, federal dockets) • News outlets: KOAM, KSNF/KODE, Read Frontier, Courthouse News • 10th Circuit Court of Appeals • Oklahoma Open Records Act requests 📋 City Records City data sourced directly from miamiok.gov — the official record, for better or worse. Visit Official Site → ⚖️ Court Records Court data from OSCN, federal databases, and public filings, with links back to the original systems whenever possible. Search Court Records → 📰 News Coverage News coverage linked to original sources so readers can compare reporting, records, and meeting material directly. View News Sources → About ExposeMiamiOK Government accountability for Miami, Oklahoma. Operated by the MoveWeight Foundation, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. We document what the city won't tell you. Contact Tips, corrections, questions: 📧 info@exposemiamiok.com Legal Not affiliated with any government entity, political campaign, or third-party group. About Miami, Oklahoma Miami (pronounced my-AM-uh) is a city in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, United States. As the county seat of Ottawa County, Miami serves as the government and commercial hub for northeastern Oklahoma. The city is located near the borders of Kansas, Missouri, and Arkansas, making it a regional center for the Four State Area. Miami is home to approximately 12,000 residents and is governed by a city council-manager form of government. Ottawa County is one of Oklahoma's 77 counties, with Miami as its county seat. The county encompasses several communities including Commerce, Quapaw, Wyandotte, Fairland, Afton, and Picher. Major highways include Interstate 44 (Will Rogers Turnpike), US-69, and US-59. Frequently Asked Questions How do I find Miami OK court records? Use our Court Records Search tool to look up cases in Ottawa County through OSCN. Or visit the Community Tools page for direct links to the Oklahoma State Courts Network. Where can I watch Miami City Council meetings? All Miami City Council and MSUA meetings are available with full transcripts at our Meeting Transcripts page. Video recordings are also hosted on our video archive and YouTube. How do I look up Ottawa County property taxes? Visit our Community Tools page for direct links to the Ottawa County Assessor's office and property record databases. How can I report government corruption in Miami OK? Use our Community Tools page to submit an anonymous report. You can also file an Open Records Request through the City of Miami or Ottawa County. records.summary: Searchable SEO text transcripts and audit review notes for Miami Oklahoma and Ottawa County finance PDFs.
records.text: Finance PDF Text Transcripts | ExposeMiamiOK A chapter of the Move Weight Foundation Follow the Money Finance PDF Text Transcripts Searchable transcripts, source PDFs, and document-review notes for the Miami, Oklahoma and Ottawa County finance archive. 81 Total PDF transcripts 24 Miami finance PDFs 57 Ottawa County PDFs 45 OCR-backed transcripts Audit Review Highlights Miami City Budget Watch FY 2025/26 total budgeted expenditures are $100,243,280. FY 2025/26 is $17,893,302 higher than FY 2024/25, a 21.73% increase. General Fund plus MSUA expenses total $61,104,580, leaving about $39,138,700 in other funds to review. General Fund revenue is only $2,117 over expenses in the budget message. MSUA revenue is $315,424 over expenses in the budget message. Community support and program subsidy line found: $1,459,457. Rainy Day Fund balance found: $5,401,439. 15 budget reports and 9 independent audit reports are now searchable. Ottawa County Money Trail Ottawa County documents now include County Commissioner Estimate of Needs files, EMS Board budgets, Board of County Health budgets, and financial statement audit PDFs. For county budgets, compare requested appropriations, cash surplus, estimated revenue, ad valorem lines, sinking fund entries, Sheriff/Jail activity, and highway/cash funds against the tax roll and SAI audit reports. Use OKTaxRolls to trace parcel-level assessed values, levies, exemptions, and tax burden changes back to budget decisions. OCR transcripts are provided for image-only PDFs, but key numbers should be checked against the original PDF images before publication or legal use. This is a public document review index, not a certified financial audit. Use it to find source documents, search text, and identify follow-up questions. Fraud, Misuse & Unsupported Spending Leads These are audit leads from official reports. They are not independent proof of criminal fraud; they are the items readers should verify first against PDFs, invoices, ledgers, bank reconciliations, purchase orders, meeting approvals, and tax-roll data. Large cash prize withdrawals lacked documentation and monitoring The city auditor reported significant cash withdrawals for prize distribution without adequate documentation, segregation of duties, oversight, or verification. The reported risk includes misappropriation, theft, loss of public funds, compliance issues, and tax-reporting problems. Miami FY 2023/24 Audit, Finding 2024-1 - open transcript Purchases were made before requisitions and purchase orders Auditors found numerous instances where invoice dates came before purchase requisitions or purchase orders, meaning purchases occurred before proper authorization. The risk noted includes unauthorized spending, budget overruns, noncompliance, fraud or abuse exposure, and possible financial misstatement. Miami FY 2023/24 Audit, Finding 2024-2 - open transcript Unresolved cash variances and unreconciled accounts continued The FY 2023/24 audit repeated the prior cash-monitoring finding. FY 2022/23 cited a duplicate $78,000 cash-transfer entry and roughly a $128,000 variance between general-ledger cash and the adjusted bank-reconciliation balance. Miami FY 2023/24 Audit, Finding 2024-4 and FY 2022/23 Finding 2023-001 - open transcript Federal reporting and procurement records were weak The city did not timely monitor CSLFRF reporting requirements and lacked a centralized grant/reporting schedule. Procurement testing also found missing evidence of required public notice for 1 of 5 CSLFRF projects tested; questioned costs were listed as $0. Miami FY 2022/23 Audit, Findings 2023-002 and 2023-003 - open transcript Ottawa County audits report unsupported or improperly charged disbursements FY 2022 reported $1,162,112 lacking adequate support, $1,125,000 not made for the proper amount, $1,133,179 charged to the wrong period, and an $80,000 vendor payment not approved by BOCC/management. FY 2021 reported $493,602 lacking adequate support and $927,010 charged to the wrong fund/account. FY 2020 reported $643,657 without invoice support, $913,872 charged to the wrong fund, and $1,429,235 not encumbered before goods or services. Ottawa County FY 2022, FY 2021, and FY 2020 audit findings - open transcript Cash-bond documentation gaps create misappropriation risk The county could not provide adequate documentation to confirm that all cash bonds were deposited and paid out to the Court Clerk or arresting agency. Auditors identified inaccurate/incomplete records and misappropriation risk. Sections Community Development Floodplain Inspections New Construction Requirements & Licensing Permits Planning Zoning Community Development View on miamiok.gov → (918) 542-3539 cheadlee@miamiokla.net Overview The Community Development Department oversees the development of land within the City of Miami, in accordance with applicable federal, state, and local codes and regulations, in order to protect and promote the health, safety, and general welfare of the residents. The goal is to maintain a community that is well planned and constructed to promote the city as a desirable place to live work and invest. This team of engineers, planners, technicians, and administrative support provides various services for the city including: 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. The intent of the NFIP is to protect the natural functions of the floodplain and to educate and inform the public of risks to lives and properties from potential flooding. The NFIP provides the maps and regulatory basis for local floodplain management. It is also the primary source of insurance protection for flood prone properties. All development within the floodplain requires a Floodplain Development Permit. Roofing contractors must fill out an Application for Roofing Contractor Registration with the Oklahoma Construction Industries Board (CIB). The City of Miami requires contractors to register with the city; for specific details, please refer to the City of Miami Contractor Registration Requirements below. Note: Contractors working within or outside the city on electrical and plumbing systems that are connected to the city's electrical or water or sewer systems must be registered with the City of Miami. Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing permit/inspection fees have been reduced. Ordinance 1641 was approved establishing a penalty for non-compliance with building permit and inspection fees. The new fee structure is found below by clicking on "Inspection Fee Schedule." The ordinance explaining the penalty for non-compliance is found below by clicking on "Ordinance 1641 Establishing Penalty and Fees Building Permits (PDF)." In general, building permits are required for: Note: Separate plumbing, mechanical, and electrical systems permits are required for the installation, alteration, repair, relocation, replacement, or addition to any wiring, piping, or equipment or appliances associated with those systems. When Permits Are Not Needed In general, a permit is not needed to: paint a house (interior or exterior); hang wallpaper; replace cabinets and do similar finish work; install concrete sidewalks and patios entirely on your property; or insulate an existing building where no structural changes are made. Permits for Other Projects For all projects, whether a building permit is required or not, there may be zoning, stormwater quality, and/or floodplain requirements that may apply. Please refer to these webpages and/or the city's contacts for these services. Related Resources 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Box 1288Miami, OK 74355 Phone: 918-542-6685 Site Links Loading Visit Miami! The Planning staff works with a variety of partners to enhance the quality of life in Miami. This includes working closely with stakeholders and being involved in county and regional planning groups and community organizations. Related Resources Monday - Friday 8 a.m. - 5 p.m. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Box 1288Miami, OK 74355 Phone: 918-542-6685 Site Links Loading Visit Miami! Utilities Online Payment Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) Online Payments CivicPlus® Zoning View on miamiok.gov → (918) 542-3539 cheadlee@miamiokla.net Overview The Zoning division is responsible for responding to code compliance complaints and zoning inquiry requests, reviewing business licenses for zoning compliance, and providing the public with information regarding municipal zoning ordinances. The Zoning division reviews development applications to ensure compliance for projects relative to construction, alteration, conversion, or use of any structure or land. The division also renders final decisions, interpretation, and/or determinations on the content and application of municipal zoning ordinances. About the Board of Adjustment The Board of Adjustment is responsible for hearing qualified requests for qualified variance from strict enforcement of the zoning ordinance regulations. The Board of Adjustment also hears appeals from decision or determination made by the zoning manager. Related Resources Monday - Friday 8 a.m. - 5 p.m. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Utilities Online Payment Report Online Payments CivicPlus® Snow Removal View on miamiok.gov → (918) 542-6825 Overview The priority plan for snow removal was developed by identifying a basic system of streets and roads essential to the continuation of traffic movement. While developing this plan, the realistic capabilities of the City of Miami, such as equipment and personnel, were kept in mind. Priority routes were developed by considering traffic volume, access to emergency services, and access to primary school bus routes. Our goal is to provide snow removal to facilitate safe traffic flow for those drivers using city streets and roads. During major storms, every available piece of equipment will be deployed. Related Resources Plowing and/or Sanding of Private Property Unless there is direct benefit to the city operations or unless emergency vehicles require access to a specific location, there will be no plowing or sanding of private property with city equipment. In the event of winter weather and/or snow accumulation, city efforts will focus on clearing city streets. The clearing of private driveways, during and after plowing shall be the responsibility of each property owner. General Information The time required to clear snow and ice from roads varies depending on the following conditions: Equipment The Street Department has three salt trucks, four plows, three front-end loaders, one grader, one skid loader, and four backhoes from other departments when needed. Street Clearing Schedule School bus routes are assigned Priority 1 or 2 and given special attention. Operators will return to widen roads as conditions warrant. During a major storm, cleanup operations may be on-going for three to four days following the storm. Public health protection requires that the Division of Solid Waste provide garbage, and yard waste collection regardless of weather conditions. The exception is during an emergency situation such as heavy snow and ice. Snow Removal Responsibilities The following roads are the responsibility of the Oklahoma Department of Transportation (ODOT): The City of Miami assist ODOT with Highway 10 and Highway 69/125 that are in the city limits of Miami. There are 224 lane miles of streets in the city limits. Lane miles are the number of lanes along a road multiplied by the distance. During severe weather, the Street Division staff works in 12 hour shifts 24 hours a day, seven days a week. All Public Works divisions assist in the snow removal when needed. Plowing Procedure Upon request from emergency services (fire, medical, police) Public Works will dispatch the necessary workers and equipment to ensure that the emergency service in question can properly respond to emergency calls. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Agendas & Minutes Agendas are available prior to the meetings. Minutes are available following approval. Members The City of Miami supports a City Council / City Manager form of government. In Miami, the Mayor and City Council serve part-time and are elected on a non-partisan basis. Under the Council / Manager form of government, the City Council acts as the legislative body in establishing policy and law and the City Manager handles the day-to-day management of the City organization. Miami is divided into four wards with an even population distribution. The City Council consists of one member from each ward and a Mayor. Each member is eligible to serve three years, with elections held every year. Elections are rotated with either two council positions or the mayor up for reelection. Utilities Online Payment City Of Miami Budget Report (PDF) City Code, Charter & Ordinances Online Payments CivicPlus® Airport View on miamiok.gov → (918) 541-1018 (918) 541-2290 (918) 542-4104 (687) 116-4975 miamiokairport@miamiokla.net Overview Welcome to MIO Airport! We're thrilled to have you here and invite you to enjoy our complimentary coffee and water, available for both pilots and guests. To make your visit even more enjoyable, we offer courtesy cars so you can explore the charming town of Miami, Oklahoma. Discover fantastic local businesses and experience the warm hospitality that awaits you. Whether you're here for a short layover or an extended stay, we hope you make the most of your time with us. Whether you're wandering through the historic downtown, enjoying a performance at the Coleman Theatre, or savoring local cuisine, you'll find plenty of opportunities to make lasting memories. Our community prides itself on making visitors feel welcome, and we are eager to share our rich history, scenic landscapes, and friendly faces with you. Come and discover why Miami, Oklahoma, is a place where you’ll always feel at home. The Miami Regional Airport, situated in the northwest area of Miami, Oklahoma, spans approximately 300 acres and holds significant potential for becoming a hub of aeronautical development. As the aviation industry continues to expand, regional airports like Miami Regional can play a crucial role in fostering economic growth and innovation within their communities. By focusing on aeronautical development, the airport could attract a range of aviation-related businesses, from aircraft maintenance and repair facilities to flight training schools and aerospace manufacturing companies. This would not only create jobs and boost the local economy but also enhance the airport's infrastructure and connectivity. By investing in modern facilities and collaborating with stakeholders, Miami Regional Airport has the opportunity to transform into a dynamic center for aviation excellence. With its 28 rentable hangars and a jet pad, the airport is well-equipped to serve a range of aviation needs. The asphalt runway, designated 17/35, stretches 5,020 feet in length and 100 feet in width, offering ample space for takeoff and landing operations. This runway supports a load capacity of up to 22,000 lbs for single axle and 44,000 lbs for double axle aircraft, making it suitable for accommodating a variety of larger aircraft. This combination of facilities not only ensures efficient operations but also offers flexibility for different types of aircraft and aviation activities, catering to both private and commercial aviation demands. We also cater to all your fueling and ground service needs with both Avgas and JetA available for self-service or full-service options. We proudly accept major credit cards and FuelMaster, ensuring a seamless transaction process. Thank you for visiting us! Whether your visit was for business or leisure, we're thrilled to have had the opportunity to connect with you. We hope you found what you were looking for and enjoyed your time here. Please don't hesitate to return soon—our doors are always open, and we'd love to welcome you back. Safe travels until we meet again! Sections Animal Control Adoptable Pets Lost/Found Pet Center Low Cost Spay/Neuter Centers Local and Emergency Vets Local Rescues Wildlife Donate Animal Control View on miamiok.gov → (918) 541-2275 (616) 204-8010 (981) 578-0657 (519) 719-2087 (918) 542-6825 mwilkins@miamiokla.net Overview The Animal Shelter is located on the truck route at 725 D Street Northeast. Animal Control is available Monday through Friday 7am to 4pm. To view adoptable animals and set up an appointment click here. Appointments may be requested 7 days/ week we will do our best to accommodate everyone. By law, all pets are required to be spayed/neutered and vaccinated for rabies. Rabies vaccinations MUST be administered by a licensed veterinarian to be legally recognized. Residents may keep or own no more than five animals at one address. Speak With Animal Control When calling Animal Control you will often get an answering machine. Please leave a detailed message including a call back number. Animal Control will return your call as soon as possible. If you feel the situation is an emergency, call Miami Police Department at 918-542-5585. Report an Animal: To Report a lost or found animal click here.You may also report your lost pet to the following agencies: https://www.pawboost.com/ https://petfbi.org/ Animal Control Facebook 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Utilities Online Payment Animal Ordinances Online Payments CivicPlus® Lost/Found Pet Center View on miamiok.gov → Step One: If you have lost a pet put out food, water, its bed, or an article of your clothing. There is a good chance your pet will return. Step Two: Fill out a Lost Pet Form by clicking here. This is submitted directly to the shelter. Step Three: Spread the word. Print lost flyers. Post them around the area your pet was last seen and try going door to door. Flyers may also be taken to local vet clinics and the animal shelter. Post on personal and local Facebook pages as well. Found PetThank you so much for helping a lost pet! Note: Pets can quickly become disorderly in appearance. It is important not to assume that the pet was dumped or not loved and cared for by its family. Check for tags or injuries. If the pet has tags call or text their pet parents and set up a reunion. If they have a rabies tag from a veterinary office call and give the office the tag number. They will often contact the owners for you. Sometimes owner/pet information is stitched or handwritten directly onto the collar so make sure you check there as well. Take pet to be scanned for microchip. Most vet offices offer this service free of charge. You can also stop by the shelter, and someone can assist you. Hold the pet for 48 hours, if you have the ability. Typically, pets don’t wander too far from home and are within ¼ mile of where they are staying. Chances are someone is looking for them close to where they were found. You can also fill out a Found Pet Form (by clicking here) so the shelter staff are aware that the pet has been found. Share, Share, Share! Post the pet on Facebook as found on local pages. The Miami Police Department is located on the south side of the Miami Civic Center. Partnership With The Community The Miami Police Department is dedicated to the safety of the citizens in our great city. Miami is a city rich in diversity and a great sense of pride. Our goal is to provide the citizens of Miami with the quality service they deserve. We value the power and effectiveness of community partnerships. The Miami Police Department is always striving for innovative ways to improve our collaborative efforts with our community. Through the principles of integrity, fairness, innovation, and community partnerships, we can make Miami the safest city in Oklahoma. The course consists of 2 hour classes one night per week. This program is designed to foster a spirit of cooperation between members of the community and the police department in a friendly learning environment. Those interested in exploring the inner mechanisms of the MPD will participate in many "hands on" topics such as CPR, riding in the police cruiser during an officer's shift and a gun safety course prior to a field trip to the gun range. Each week, academy students will delve into a different aspect of police work. Students can participate as much or as little as they choose, making the academy a very stress-free and beneficial experience. You are invited to join the Miami Police Department's 5th Annual Citizen's Academy September 7th to October 26th, 2017. The MPD and Chief "H.T." Anderson would like to invite area citizens to participate in the Academy. This class has been designed to build a bond of mutual trust and respect between the police department and our citizens and to bring the police and community closer together in a setting that offers both training and understanding to each participant. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Utilities Online Payment Online Payments CivicPlus® Divisions View on miamiok.gov → (800) 522-3511 (918) 542-3898 (918) 541-2314 (186) 845-5927 ssigmon@miamiokla.net Dispatch / Communications Our Dispatch Center is operational 24 hours a day, seven days a week and is the answering point for all 9-1-1 calls in Ottawa County as well as the dispatch center for several other communities for police, fire, and ambulance. Our duties include telephone communications, radio dispatch, and operating the law enforcement teletype computer. The teletype is used to access information for law enforcement officers to use such as drivers license information, vehicle registration and to check if a vehicle is stolen, or if a person may be wanted by the police. Our job, primarily, is to receive calls for assistance, and then relay the information given to us to the appropriate service for response. Detective Division The Detective Division is comprised of five detectives. Three detectives are assigned to day shift, one to evening shift, and the fifth investigates drug crimes. The detectives have a scheduled rotation to provide coverage during off hours. Patrol Division The Miami Police Department refers to its Patrol Division as the "Operations Division." Operations is the primary provider of police services for the residents of Miami. It deploys 21 officers to approximately 9.71 square miles of the city on a 24-hour basis. Operations personnel are prepared to respond to both emergency and non-emergency calls for service in each of the city's patrol districts. The patrol area is comprised of four districts. The division is commanded by a police captain and each shift is supervised by a police sergeant and corporal. Records The records clerk has the responsibility of accurately processing and maintaining all departmental reports (i.e., traffic citations, offense complaints, accident reports to allow for easy access and review). The clerk must assure the safety and confidentiality of all law enforcement records. The records clerk also assists the public and other agencies in obtaining copies of the proper reports they request to see. The clerk also maintains accurate Uniform Crime Report (UCR) records that are sent in to the State of Oklahoma by keeping totals and types of crimes committed within the police department's jurisdiction. The purpose of the Citizen Police Academy is to foster a spirit of cooperation and understanding between members of the community and the police department in a friendly learning environment. This class has been designed to build a bond of mutual trust and respect between the Police Department and our citizens and to bring the police and community closer together in a setting that offers both training and understanding to each participant. Additionally, the academy highlights the importance of citizen participation in public safety by educating the public about their own awareness as concerned citizens so that we may continue to work together towards making our community the safest possible. Those interested in exploring the inner mechanisms of the Miami Police Department will participate in many "hands on" topics such as learning CPR, experience riding in a police cruiser, and how police respond to calls and motor vehicle accidents. Participation also includes one Saturday field trip to the gun range to learn firearms safety with live fire. Chaplain Corps The Miami Police Department has established a Chaplain Corps to serve the men and women of the Police Department and the citizens of Miami by providing pastoral and/or support services to the department's personnel and city citizens in crisis situations. The Chaplain Corps seeks, as one of its goals, to promote a positive relationship between the Police Department, the City of Miami, and community members. Reserve Officer Program In order to supplement patrol forces, MPD trains, equips, and deploys reserve police officers to assist with the needs of the Police Department. These officers must work by the same guidelines and laws as regular full time officers. Reserve officers are generally not compensated; however, circumstances may allow payment for certain duties. Ride-a-Long Program The Miami Police Department provides a Citizen Ride-a-Long Program to form a closer relationship and better understanding with the citizens of the community. Members of the community who meet certain minimal criteria may participate in the Ride-a-Long Program by accompanying participating officers on their shifts. The legislature further finds that the privacy interest of persons adjudicated guilty of these crimes is less important than the state's interest in public safety. The legislature additionally finds that a system of registration will permit law enforcement officials to identify and alert the public when necessary for protecting public safety. State Of Oklahoma All sex offenders, as defined in 57 O.S. Supp. 2008, Section 582, have a duty to register with the local law enforcement authority having jurisdiction in the area where the person intends to reside or to stay for more than seven days in accordance with Oklahoma State Statute 57 O.S. Supp 1997, Section 583. If a sex offender changes address, the offender shall notify the appropriate agencies in writing no later than three days before the offender establishes residence or is temporarily domiciled at the new address. Out of State If the sex offender changes address to another state, the offender shall register the new address with the appropriate agencies in the new state not later than 10 days before the offender establishes residency or is temporarily domiciled in the new state, if the new state has a registration requirement. The Miami Police Department only provides registration information for offenders living within the city limits of Miami, Oklahoma. It is the job of the school resource officers to patrol all school campuses, investigate criminal activity and traffic accidents, educate students and staff about crime prevention, and participate in other various programs and activities on all Miami Public School campuses. This is a vital position for our department and the program has been a great success. The goal of the program is to make our public schools as safe as possible and provide a positive learning environment for all students. Funding These positions are funded by the City of Miami. The school resource officers works closely with school administration, staff, students and parents to handle the variety of issues that arise on the school campuses. Our School Resource Officers have received specialized training for the assignment and continues to obtain additional training when budget and time allows. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Utilities Online Payment Online Payments CivicPlus® Educational Brochures and Flyers View on miamiok.gov → Overview Stormwater pollution from point sources and nonpoint sources is a challenging water quality problem. Unlike pollution from industry or sewage treatment facilities, which is caused by a discrete number of sources, stormwater pollution is caused by the daily activities of people everywhere. Rainwater and snowmelt run off streets, lawns, farms, and construction and industrial sites and pick up fertilizers, dirt, pesticides, oil and grease, and many other pollutants on the way to our rivers, lakes, and coastal waters. Stormwater runoff is our most common cause of water pollution. Because stormwater pollution is caused by so many different activities, traditional regulatory controls will only go so far. Education and outreach are key components to any successful stormwater program. Educational Brochures and Flyers Resources Below is a list of, but not limited to, Organizations that have constructed and supplied the Brochures and Flyers. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Most nonpoint sources are related to land use activities. For example, rainwater washes over farmlands and carries topsoil and residues from farm chemicals into nearby streams. Primary nonpoint sources of water pollution include runoff from agriculture, urban areas, mining, forestry and construction activities. Pollution prevention, as it relates to NPS pollution, starts with understanding how everyday human activities affect the quality of air, land and water. This has been intended to educate students in kindergarten through ninth grade to help them understand the definition of water pollution using the basic principles of science, mathematics, fun and games. Sections Fire Department Fire Prevention Tips Department Tours / Smoke Alarm Information Fire Department View on miamiok.gov → (918) 542-3472 cchenoweth@miamiokla.net abass@miamiokla.net Overview The Miami Fire Department (MFD) provides fire suppression services, emergency medical services, hazardous materials mitigation at the operations level, and rescue technician level services within the City of Miami's 45-square-mile response area. The MFD came into existence as a volunteer fire department in 1905, and was established as a full-time paid department in 1910. Jess Kern was the fire chief, Herman Beck and Glen Kern were firefighters. They were on duty 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Their salary was a mere $40 per week. Since 1910, the department has grown from three full-time fire personnel and one fire station to 28 firefighters and two fire stations servicing a population of more than 13,500 residents. Currently, the City of Miami enjoys an ISO rating of 3. Department Mission The mission of the Miami Fire Department shall be to protect lives and property from fires, medical emergencies, and all natural and man-made disasters. We will respond in a professional, courteous, and timely manner, providing our customers with the highest level of public service. We shall reduce the rate and severity of emergencies through continuous training, public education, fire prevention, and disaster management services. To maintain the great public trust bestowed upon us, we shall adhere to the highest ethical standards in all we do. Resources Monday - Friday 7:00 a.m. - 5:30 p.m. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Our dedicated fire department personnel go to great lengths to ensure your group has an informative as well as enjoyable experience. If you are a senior, we will come by your home and check the operation of your smoke detectors, replace one if need be, and provide you with any other recommendations that we determine will reduce your risk for fire or other life safety concerns. Free Smoke Alarms The Miami Fire Department currently offers a free smoke alarm to anyone that needs one. These smoke alarms can be procured by calling Fire Department Administration Headquarters at 918-542-6685 or 918-542-4164. Once your contact information is attained, we will send Fire Department personnel to install a smoke detector in your home. Smoke Alarm Maintenance Remember to change your detector battery when you change your clock. Some newer alarms have a special battery that you don't have to change. Instead you replace the detector itself. Smoke alarms can become dusty or otherwise malfunction over time. Your average smoke alarm should be changed every three to five years (per manufactures recommendations). Install smoke alarms on every level of the building, including the basement, and in every bedroom. The alarm can be placed on the ceiling or on the wall; however, it is recommended that it be placed on the ceiling. The alarm should be no less than six" from corners. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Sections Emergency Management Emergency Preparedness Finding a Safe Location Preparing a Disaster Supply Kit Recovery Programs Emergency Management View on miamiok.gov → (914) 536-6118 Overview The City's Emergency Management department knows the likelihood of you and your family recovering from an emergency tomorrow depends on the planning and preparation you do today. While everyone's abilities and needs are unique, every individual can take steps to prepare for all kinds of emergencies. These emergencies can be from fires, severe weather, flooding, and other natural and/or man made hazard events. By looking at your own personnel needs and making an emergency plan that fits those needs, you and your family can be better prepared to face what might come your way. Preparing makes sense for everyone. The American Red Cross has a free Tornado App for iPhone and Android. It will inform you of tornado warnings and watches and severe weather in your area. It also provides information such as what to do before and after a tornado and what you should do to prepare for one. The app lets your phone function as a flashlight, strobe light, alarm, etc. and will allow you to communicate with others to let them know if you are safe or need assistance. Knowing the difference between watches and warnings can help save lives. After the Storm Once severe weather has passed, be prepared for possible flooding to occur. Also, watch for downed power lines and never drive into high water. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Box 1288Miami, OK 74355 Phone: 918-542-6685 Site Links Loading Visit Miami! Utilities Online Payment Emergency Preparedness Guide Online Payments CivicPlus® Finding a Safe Location View on miamiok.gov → Identifying Your Safest Place at Home / Work Before an emergency strikes, take time to identify your safest place at home, at work, and at school. Many people have survived strong tornadoes in a closet or small interior room without windows. Usually the safest place will be on the lowest floor. If you live in a mobile home, identify the nearest sturdy building - it may not be safe to remain in a mobile home during a storm. Safety Elsewhere At schools, offices, and hospitals, preparedness plans are especially important due to the large number of people on hand and the large amount of glass at many sites. Know the safest place for you to shelter in place and make sure others know their assigned location as well. At shopping malls, indoor pools, and gymnasiums, long spanning buildings are commonly found. These locations can be dangerous because the entire roof can be supported by the outside walls. If caught in such an open building, the restroom may be the best place to take shelter. Safe Rooms If possible, one of the best ways to prepare for survival in Tornado Alley states like Oklahoma is to build or install a safe rooms in your home or workplace. Your local emergency manager or home builders association will have information about safe rooms. Plan how to get to your safest place, and share the information with your family. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Box 1288Miami, OK 74355 Phone: 918-542-6685 Site Links Loading Visit Miami! Utilities Online Payment Online Payments CivicPlus® Preparing a Disaster Supply Kit View on miamiok.gov → What to Pack Electricity, water, heat, air conditioning, or telephone service may not work in an emergency. Preparing disaster supply kits in advance can save precious time in the event you must evacuate or go without utilities for an extended period. Store items for a "go" kit in an easy-to-carry bag and keep in a car or in the garage. The "home" kit can be stored in a plastic tub or garbage can and kept in your home's safest place where you will take shelter. Utilities Online Payment Online Payments CivicPlus® Recovery Programs View on miamiok.gov → (918) 542-7133 Disaster recovery consists of the actions taken by a community to return to normal or near-normal conditions. It often includes the restoring of basic services and repairing of physical, social, and economic damages. Typical recovery actions will include debris cleanup, financial assistance to individuals and to city governments, and sustaining mass care for human and animal populations that are displaced because of the disaster. Disaster recovery typically occurs in phases beginning with efforts to help those affected meet immediate needs for housing, food, and water. As those needs are met and people continue to repair their homes and businesses and return to work, long term recovery begins to take place. Long term recovery consists of the continuance of cleanup and rebuilding efforts of roads, bridges, and key facilities with the help and support of government agencies, voluntary organizations, and the private sector. Due to how severe the impacts of the disaster, considerable interagency coordination and technical support may be required. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. Sections Civil Rights Program Policy Local, State, & Federal Resources Community Resources Community Area Maps Community Health Information Demographics History Of Miami Miami's Commitment To Excellence Civil Rights Program Policy View on miamiok.gov → The City of Miami (City) is committed to ensuring that no person is excluded from participation in, denied the benefits of, or subjected to discrimination under any program, activity, or service that it provides. The City will not tolerate intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination against any individual or group. This policy establishes a framework for taking reasonable steps to ensure access to all services provided by the City for all citizens and establishes procedures whereby the City will receive and investigate allegations of discrimination. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 is the overarching civil rights law that prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, in any program, service, or activity that receives federal assistance. Specifically, Title VI assures that “No person in the United States shall, on the grounds of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefit of, or be otherwise subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving federal assistance.” Nondiscrimination prohibitions have been further broadened and supplemented by related statutes, regulations, and executive orders. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 (Title IX), which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in any education or training program receiving federal financial assistance, with a limited number of defined exceptions; • Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Section 504), which forbids discrimination on the basis of an individual's disability by all federal agencies and in all federally funded activities; • The Age Discrimination Act of 1975, as amended, which prohibits discrimination in federally supported activities on the basis of age. The City is actively engaged in Title VI activities as a recipient of federal assistance from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The City will not restrict an individual in any way from the enjoyment of any advantage or privilege enjoyed by others receiving any service, financial aid, or other benefit under any of its programs, regardless of the funding source for the program. Individuals may not be subjected to criteria or methods of administration which cause adverse impact because of their race, color, or national origin, or have the effect of defeating or substantially impairing accomplishment of the objectives of the program because of race, color, or national origin. The City will not tolerate intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination against any individual or group for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege guaranteed under law or regulations, or because the individual has filed a complaint or has testified, assisted, or participated in any way in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing or has opposed any City action or decision. The City will take reasonable measures, when available, to provide access to City services to individuals with limited ability to speak, write, or understand English and/or to those with disabilities. The City’s Nondiscrimination Program Plan and Policy may be found by clicking here: Filing a Complaint If someone believes they have suffered from discrimination under a City of Miami service programs, they may contact the City of Miami Nondiscrimination Program Coordinator to seek informal resolution. If the matter cannot be resolved informally, the following steps will be followed: • Within 180 days of the alleged discrimination, complainants may submit a written or verbal complaint to the Nondiscrimination Program Coordinator. Complaints must include the complainant’s name, the nature of the complaint, the dates of the complaint, requested action, and contact information. Complaint forms are available in here. • The Nondiscrimination Program Coordinator will review the complaint and may solicit additional information from the complainant as needed. If additional information is requested and not received, the case may be closed. The case may also be closed if the complainant no longer wishes to pursue their case. • If the complaint is outside the jurisdiction of the City, the complainant will be notified of the name and contact information for the appropriate agency with jurisdiction, if known. Complaint Processing If the complaint is within the jurisdiction of the City, or informal resolution was not possible, it will be promptly and impartially investigated. The City’s goal is to address complaints within 60 days of receipt, though the time to carefully investigate complaints may be longer depending on the nature of the complaint and complexity of the issue. Preliminary Inquiry: • The City will conduct a preliminary inquiry to determine the need for further investigation. • The City will notify the complainant in writing that a preliminary inquiry is underway to determine the need for further investigation. • If the preliminary inquiry by the City indicates that an investigation is warranted, the complainant will be notified in writing and an interview will be scheduled. • If the preliminary inquiry indicates an investigation is not warranted, the complainant will be notified in writing of the reasons why and factors considered. Complaint Investigation: • Complaints warranting further investigation will be promptly and impartially processed by the City Nondiscrimination Program Coordinator. The results of the investigation will be provided to the City Manager for review. • The complainant will be notified in writing of the results of the investigation and what actions will be/have been taken in response and a timeline to request review. Wayland C. Lykins, the son of a missionary to the Peoria Indians, came to the area to raise cattle in the 1890s. He had a dream of a cattle empire with his town, Miami, as the hub. Lykins went to Washington D.C. for congressional approval of a town site. It was only after Thomas F. Richardville, chief of the Miami Tribe and friend of Lykins, spoke to U.S. Indian Commissioner that the township patent was approved. The Ottawa Tribe sold 588 acres for the town, and the first lot was sold to Dr. WI. McWilliams in June of 1891. Dr. McWilliams received the first deed to a white man in Indian Territory, and the town was named Miami, "My-Am-Uh," after the Miami Indians. Miami grew from a population of 300 that first year to around 2,500 by 1902. Many factors contributed to its growth. The rolling prairie was good pastureland for cattle, and the area was becoming widely known for its shipments of hay. The first train arrived in Miami on September 12, 1896, the Kansas City, Fort Scott and Memphis Railway Company, which connected Miami to Baxter Springs, Kansas. This line continued until 1900 when it was extended south to Afton to meet the Frisco mainline. Lead and zinc were first discovered in the area in 1905. Mining operations were running by 1907 in the "Commerce field" and extended to the "Picher and Cardin fields" in 1915 to 1916. Miami became the gateway to these mining fields, therefore mining became a dominant part of Miami's growth. The need for training of mining engineers resulted in the School of Mines opening in 1919. This school evolved into present day Northeastern Oklahoma A&M College. By 1909, Miami had 9 miles of cement walks, one 3-story brick hotel, three bakeries, three newspapers, a modern waterworks system, a modernly equipped fire department, electric lights, big ice plant, 13 churches, two railroads, three banks, planning mills, lumber yards, and splendid public schools. With the burst of mining the prairie town that Lykins envisioned was becoming a booming trade center. A vaudeville theatre and movie palace "Coleman Theatre Beautiful" opened to a full house of 1600 on April 18, 1929. Built by George L. Coleman, Sr., local mining magnate, the opulent structure with Spanish Mission Revival exterior and Louis XV interior design dazzled the audiences. From that day forward the Coleman has never been "dark." The theatre has been fully restored and truly is a jewel of Route 66. The Pensacola Dam was constructed from 1938 to 1940 across the Grand (or Neosho) River at the Grand River Valley. This dam provided both electricity to the area and jobs for many during the hard times of the Great Depression. The damming of the river created Grand Lake ‘O the Cherokees, providing recreational activities for people living in the area and visiting tourists. Manufacturing, on a large scale, came to Miami in 1946, with the opening of B.F. Goodrich Miami Plant. Soon to follow were Blue Manufacturing Company opening in 1953 and U.S. Metal Container moving to Miami in 1955. Many manufacturers still call Miami home today. Located in the northern part of town is a G.A.R. (Grand Army of the Republic) Cemetery, which includes Civil War era grave sites and British Flyers, who trained in Miami for WWII who tragically lost their lives during flights. Historic Route 66 is still Main Street here in Miami, and many of the buildings in downtown are originals from the early 1900s. Ten Native American tribes are located in or near Miami; Quapaw Tribe, Wyandotte Tribe, Modoc Tribe, Miami Tribe, Seneca-Cayuga Tribe, Ottawa Tribe, Eastern Shawnee Tribe, Peoria Tribe, Shawnee Tribe, and the Cherokee Tribe. The Dobson Museum, located near downtown, displays local Native American artifacts and has over 5,000 historical items. Tourism has become a huge part of the community. Many Indian gaming facilities, Route 66 attractions, numerous art murals, and downtown Main Street lure visitors to Miami. When spring rolls around, fisherman line the banks of the Neosho River hoping to snag a spoonbill, sometimes called a paddlefish. While visiting Miami, don’t forget to take our Miami Downtown Historic Walking Tour and take in all the history Miami has to offer along with the beautiful architecture. 129 5th Avenue NWP.O. records.summary: $33 Million Verdict: Ottawa County Jail Death of Terral Ellis Jr. | ExposeMiamiOK A chapter of the Move Weight Foundation ExposeMiamiOK - Community Resources & Transparency ← Back to Home ← Back to Blog Wrongful Death $33 Million Verdict Upheld: Ottawa County Jail Death of Terral Ellis Jr. April 21-24, 2026 | Sources:
records.text: $33 Million Verdict: Ottawa County Jail Death of Terral Ellis Jr. | ExposeMiamiOK A chapter of the Move Weight Foundation ExposeMiamiOK - Community Resources & Transparency ← Back to Home ← Back to Blog Wrongful Death $33 Million Verdict Upheld: Ottawa County Jail Death of Terral Ellis Jr. April 21-24, 2026 | Sources: 10th Circuit Court of Appeals, KOAM, Read Frontier, Courthouse News The 10th Circuit Court of Appeals has upheld a $33 million verdict against Ottawa County in the wrongful death of Terral Ellis Jr., age 26, who died of sepsis and pneumonia on October 22, 2015, while in custody at the Ottawa County Jail. What Happened According to court records and news coverage from Courthouse News , Ellis turned himself in on October 10, 2015. Over the next 12 days, jail staff allegedly ignored, mocked, and ridiculed him as he pleaded for medical attention. Video evidence shows Ellis begging for help for 20 hours before his death . The Verdict A jury awarded the Ellis family $33 million in damages. The 10th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld this verdict in April 2026, rejecting Ottawa County's appeal. Taxpayer Impact: The judgment has grown to approximately $40 million with interest . Ottawa County officials have publicly discussed municipal bankruptcy and property tax increases as potential solutions. The county could spread payments over 10 years (~$5M/year). Court Records & News Coverage KOAM News Read Frontier Courthouse News KSNF/KODE FourStatesHomepage Why This Matters This case represents one of the largest civil rights verdicts in Oklahoma history and highlights systemic failures in jail medical care. The $40 million burden falls on Ottawa County taxpayers, many of whom are already struggling with economic challenges. The case also raises questions about accountability and oversight in county jail operations across Oklahoma. records.text: Mayor Bless Parker Evidence File: Vance Posts, Complaint, Public Records | ExposeMiamiOK A chapter of the Move Weight Foundation ExposeMiamiOK - Community Resources & Transparency ← Back to Home Back to Blog Evidence File Mayor Bless Parker Evidence File: Vance Posts, Criminal Complaint, Public Records Questions Updated May 31, 2026 | Sources: screenshots supplied from public Facebook posts, complaint pages, OML page captures, Miami/Ottawa public records leads This page organizes the public screenshots and complaint pages now in the evidence file concerning Bless Parker, Mayor of Miami, Oklahoma . It separates what the screenshots show from what remains an allegation that needs to be matched against official records. Evidence standard: Screenshots and complaint pages are leads, not court findings. The next step is matching each claim to city agendas, minutes, contracts, emails, ORA responses, social-media archives, law-enforcement case records, and employment/compensation records. 1. Official-Page Commercial Promotion Questions Several provided screenshots show posts from pages labeled Bless Parker or Bless Parker Mayor of Miami Oklahoma promoting or sharing posts for John Vance Auto Group and related dealerships in Miami. April 9, 2025: screenshot text says, "Let's Bless Your Ride! Employee Pricing at the Ford/Lincoln and Dodge/Jeep/Chrysler/Ram stores. Give me a call or text at 918-541-8839." April 25, 2025: screenshot shows a Bless Parker post sharing a Vance Fleet Services item and referencing Vance Chevy Buick GMC of Miami, Vance Ford-Lincoln, and Vance Dodge Chrysler Jeep Ram. May 9, 2025: screenshot shows a Bless Parker post congratulating a customer on a 2026 Chevy Equinox purchase and thanking them for staying local with Vance Chevy Buick. May 23, 2025: screenshots show "Come see me or shoot me a text 918-541-8839" and "Give me a call or text 918-541-8839 and Let's Bless Your Ride! #blessyourride" attached to John Vance Auto Group material. The public-records question is whether these posts were made on an official government page, whether they constitute public records, whether any were deleted after records requests or press inquiries, and whether the mayor's private employment or compensation created a conflict of interest. 2. Citizen Criminal Complaint Filed April 21, 2026 The complaint pages provided identify the complainant as Ronald Edward Durbin II of Guerrilla.News / Guerrilla Publishing and list the receiving agency as the Miami Police Department, City of Miami, Oklahoma. The complaint identifies the primary subject as Bless Parker, Mayor, City of Miami, Oklahoma, and lists bparker@miamiokla.net as the subject email. The complaint identifies Parker's subject employer as John Vance Auto Group / Vance Chevrolet Buick GMC, 1601 N. Main Street, Miami, Oklahoma 74354 . It alleges multiple categories of misconduct. These remain allegations unless confirmed by investigative findings or court records. 3. Counts And Statutes Alleged In The Complaint Count One: alleged felony misuse of official position for personal financial gain, citing 21 O.S. 365, 21 O.S. 381, and 21 O.S. 341. Count Two: alleged willful destruction of public records subject to the Oklahoma Open Records Act, citing 51 O.S. 24A.17(A), 51 O.S. 24A.3, and 21 O.S. 540. Count Three: alleged willful disclosure of executive-session proceedings, citing 25 O.S. 307 and 25 O.S. 314. Count Four: alleged official oppression, intimidation, and retaliation against private citizens and public employees, citing 21 O.S. 567 and First Amendment concerns. Conspiracy allegation: the complaint also references 21 O.S. 341 in connection with alleged coordinated conduct. 4. Open Records And Deleted-Post Preservation Issue The complaint states that on or about April 20, 2026 , an Open Records Act request was served on the City of Miami seeking records associated with Mayor Parker's official government Facebook page, including posts, commercial solicitations, deletions, and related content. It further alleges that after the ORA request and active reporting, one or more posts were deleted from the official "Mayor of Miami Oklahoma" Facebook page. The key record-preservation issue is whether Meta/Facebook records, city-device records, page admin logs, screenshots, and city email can confirm what existed, when it was deleted, and who controlled the page. 5. Executive Session And Retaliation Allegations The complaint alleges recorded audio exists concerning direct communications between Durbin and Mayor Parker about Miami City Council executive-session subject matter. It also alleges retaliation or intimidation directed at people believed to be sources, including City Attorney Misty Fields Barnes. Records to check include executive-session agenda items, required minutes or post-session records, council meeting video, public-comment records, city attorney employment records, text-message metadata, and the audio referenced in the complaint. 6. Personal-Life Screenshots Some provided screenshots show public posts by Parker and Kendra Parker about private marital issues. This page does not repeat sensitive personal-health allegations. Those screenshots are relevant only to the extent they help establish a timeline of public statements, deleted posts, retaliation claims, or the authenticity/control of public Facebook pages. 7. Strip Club / Sade Bass Allegation A provided public Facebook screenshot attributed to Kendra Parker states that it was "not a one night stand," names Sade Bass, alleges $3,600 was paid for Parker and four mayors to enter a champagne room, and asks what was received for that payment. This is an allegation from a screenshot. The records question is whether any public money, campaign money, municipal travel, official event, reimbursement, or other public nexus exists. 8. Ottawa County Jail Judgment Context A supplied Miami News-Record screenshot says the Ottawa County Board of Commissioners scheduled a special meeting at 1 p.m. Tuesday, May 19 , in the Civic Center banquet room at 129 5th Ave. in Miami , concerning the Austin Bond v. Sheriff of Ottawa County judgment. The screenshot reports a $33 million verdict related to the 2015 death in custody of Terral Ellis II and says officials were expected to discuss financing options including a limited sales-tax-backed bond, a 10-year levy, a three-year unlimited ad valorem levy, or possible bankruptcy. The screenshot says no votes would be taken and that Miami News-Record would livestream the meeting. 9. OML Board And Public Contact Context Provided screenshots from the Oklahoma Municipal League site list board meeting information at 201 N.E. 23rd Street, Oklahoma City, OK 73105 , phone 405-528-7515 , and show Bless Parker, Mayor, Miami as District 1. Another provided city contact screenshot lists the Miami mayor and council contacts, including Mayor Bless Parker at 918-542-9251 . 10. Records To Pull Next Full Facebook/Meta preservation package for the "Mayor of Miami Oklahoma" page, including deleted posts, admin logs, timestamps, and page-role history. City of Miami ORA request and response logs for April 2026 requests involving Parker, Vance Auto Group, Facebook posts, city email, texts, and financial records. Employment, compensation, and conflict-disclosure records involving Parker and John Vance Auto Group. City council agendas, minutes, video, executive-session entries, and public comments for April 2026. Any Miami Police Department, Ottawa County Sheriff's Department, District Attorney, or OSBI case number or referral record connected to the complaint. Ottawa County commissioners meeting records and livestream/video for the special jail-judgment meeting. Status The provided screenshots have been read into a structured evidence timeline. The previous noisy screenshot dump generated from Facebook search scrolling has been removed from the site. Future additions should be clean exhibits with clear dates, source labels, and a direct records question attached. Message Fiscal Year (FY) 2026/2027 June 2, 2026 To the Honorable Mayor, City Council and Citizens of Miami: The City of Miami’s Fiscal Year 2026/2027 Budget reflects our continued commitment to responsible spending, quality public services, infrastructure investment, and long-term financial stability. The General Fund, supported primarily by sales tax and utility revenues, remains essential to funding core services such as police, fire, public works, risk management, and administration. At the same time, the Miami Special Utility Authority (MSUA) continues to move forward with major infrastructure investments, including AMI metering, water system improvements, a new water tower, and the development of an MSUA-owned high-speed fiber system. Balancing these priorities requires careful planning. The City must continue providing reliable services today while preserving reserves, preparing for future needs, and investing in projects that support growth and quality of life. The Rainy Day Fund remains an important safeguard for economic uncertainty, and citywide street maintenance continues to be a priority as rising costs create ongoing challenges. The FY 2026/2027 Budget includes $82,728,742.05 in total expenditures. General Fund revenues are budgeted at $22,229,519 with expenses at $22,219,688. MSUA revenues are budgeted at $44,424,640 with expenses budgeted at $44,254,413. Throughout the past year, City departments continued to provide essential services, complete major projects, and support the daily needs of residents, businesses, and visitors. Community and Economic Development The Convention and Visitors Bureau, Miami Main Street, and the Route 66 Centennial Committee continued planning for the Route 66 Centennial, including Heritage Fest, Tri-State Cruise Night, and an Airstream show. Miami Main Street continued to support downtown activity through events such as Sip N’ Shops, Sweet Street, and the annual Holiday Market. A Route 66 grant brought new wayfinding signs to Main Street, and Miami was selected to host a National Main Street Conference Mobile Workshop, bringing Main Street directors from across the country to the community. City of Miami Budget Message FY 2026/2027 Page 5 of 17 61 Packet Page 62 Miami also saw continued growth through new businesses, expansions, and community investments, including restaurants, retail, entertainment, professional services, tribal projects, housing improvements, and community facilities. Public Utilities and MSUA MSUA continued work on several significant infrastructure projects. Trustees approved contracts for the construction of an MSUA-owned and operated high-speed fiber optic system, with the goal of beginning service to residential, commercial, and industrial customers by the end of 2026. The AMI metering project also moved forward through a $6.8 million Oklahoma Water Resources Board (OWRB) grant funded by the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). This project, completed in partnership with the Modoc Tribe and Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma, will improve service reliability and efficiency for MSUA utility customers. Additional utility improvements include a $2.1 million Water Treatment Plant project for new pumps, piping, and valves, as well as a new $2.6 million, 400,000-gallon water tower. The new tower will improve water supply reliability and provide redundancy for customers east of the turnpike and industrial users. Public Works and Municipal Operations Parks and cemetery improvements included a new concession stand at Splash Pad Park, restoration of the iconic slide at Rocket Park, and the addition of a Scatter Garden and Ossuary at G.A.R. Cemetery. The Miami Animal Control and Shelter continued expanding services and community impact. Gross animal intake for calendar year 2025 reached 510 animals, a 21% increase over 2024. Since July 1, 2025, the shelter has provided temporary care for more than 345 animals, including approximately 215 cats and 130 dogs. During that time, 46 animals were adopted, 15 dogs were returned to owners, and 117 animals were transferred to rescue and partner organizations. The shelter also maintained an average 94% live release rate and was officially recognized as a “No-Kill” facility. These are audit leads and questions, not findings of wrongdoing.
